prompt:
I'm modelling a small gold nanorod as a prolate spheroid with semi-axes 10 nm x 10 nm x 25 nm, in water, with light polarised along the long axis (propagating perpendicular to it). At what wavelength does its longitudinal plasmon peak in extinction, somewhere between 550 and 750 nm? Johnson & Christy data for the gold is fine.

---
Report your result by calling submit_answer with these values:
- `peak_wavelength_nm` (nm): vacuum wavelength of maximum extinction

concerns: I took water as a constant, real index of n = 1.33.
The 639 nm value comes from a full-wave boundary-element (BEM) solve with a mesh of about 2 nm (1,620 triangles) and 1 nm wavelength steps. I didn't check it on a finer mesh, so allow about ±2–3 nm.

The quasistatic (electrostatic) model puts the peak at 628 nm, but the tool warned it's unreliable for a particle this size (size parameter 0.38). The ~10 nm red-shift in the full-wave result is expected.

A discrete-dipole (DDA) check gave 670 nm, but it used only 352 dipoles (a 6×6×16 grid), which is far too coarse for this shape. Its peak height also disagreed with BEM by several-fold, so I didn't use it.
The particle is modelled as an ideal spheroid. Real nanorods are closer to capped cylinders and would peak at a somewhat different wavelength.
answer.summary: The longitudinal plasmon of the 10 × 10 × 25 nm gold spheroid in water peaks in extinction at about 639 nm (Johnson & Christy gold, n = 1.33, field along the long axis, light travelling perpendicular to it). This comes from a full-wave boundary-element (BEM) calculation with no warnings. At the peak the extinction cross-section is about 1.10 × 10⁴ nm² (Q_ext ≈ 19), and absorption makes up about 90% of it. The peak is about 25 nm wide at half maximum. The simpler quasistatic model gives 628 nm; the ~10 nm red-shift in the full-wave result is expected for a rod this length.

result.conventions:
Lightsmith conventions (fixed; changing them needs a schema version bump):
- Lengths in nm. Wavelengths are vacuum wavelengths in nm.
- Time dependence exp(-i omega t): absorbing materials have Im(eps) > 0 and Im(n) > 0.
- Cross sections in nm^2; efficiencies Q = C / (pi r_eq^2), r_eq = volume-equivalent radius of all particles.
- layer_stack / periodic: layers listed from the superstrate (incidence side) to the substrate; light travels +z.
  R is measured in the superstrate, T in the substrate.
- mode: cross-section in the xy plane, propagation along +z.
- device: ports are planes whose normal is the axis where size_nm is zero; direction is into the device.
- problem.options[<method or backend name>] holds solver options, validated by that backend.
- Materials: {"kind": "constant_index", "n_real": .., "n_imag": ..}, {"kind": "library", "name": "Au"},
  drude, drude_lorentz, tabulated, constant_permittivity. FDTD needs dispersive models (fit_drude_lorentz).
- Results carry provenance and warnings: read the warnings before trusting the numbers.

content.thinking:
I'm noting that the DDA model uses only 352 dipoles on a coarse 6x6x16 grid, so its shape representation is distorted and I don't trust it much. The BEM result with a 2 nm mesh looks credible, and a rough quasistatic check with radiative correction puts the red peak near 639 nm, which is plausible. I'm considering whether a finer BEM mesh would be a useful convergence check.

I'm settling on a 2 nm mesh for the 10 nm radius, which seems reasonable, and I'll report 639 nm as the red peak.

The longitudinal plasmon peak lands at about 639 nm (roughly 627–652 nm at half maximum) in the full-wave BEM result, with the quasistatic and DDA cross-checks agreeing only loosely. The DDA mesh was too coarse to trust, so I'm setting it aside.

concerns: I took water as a constant, real index of n = 1.33.
The 639 nm value comes from a full-wave boundary-element (BEM) solve with a mesh of about 2 nm (1,620 triangles) and 1 nm wavelength steps. I didn't check it on a finer mesh, so allow about ±2–3 nm.

The quasistatic (electrostatic) model puts the peak at 628 nm, but the tool warned it's unreliable for a particle this size (size parameter 0.38). The ~10 nm red-shift in the full-wave result is expected.

A discrete-dipole (DDA) check gave 670 nm, but it used only 352 dipoles (a 6×6×16 grid), which is far too coarse for this shape. Its peak height also disagreed with BEM by several-fold, so I didn't use it.
The particle is modelled as an ideal spheroid. Real nanorods are closer to capped cylinders and would peak at a somewhat different wavelength.
input.summary: The longitudinal plasmon of the 10 × 10 × 25 nm gold spheroid in water peaks in extinction at about 639 nm (Johnson & Christy gold, n = 1.33, field along the long axis, light travelling perpendicular to it). This comes from a full-wave boundary-element (BEM) calculation with no warnings. At the peak the extinction cross-section is about 1.10 × 10⁴ nm² (Q_ext ≈ 19), and absorption makes up about 90% of it. The peak is about 25 nm wide at half maximum. The simpler quasistatic model gives 628 nm; the ~10 nm red-shift in the full-wave result is expected for a rod this length.
